title: Apartment Marketing Plan for 2027: What to Plan and Budget For, by Channel and Lease Stage
seoTitle: Apartment Marketing Plan for 2027, by Channel and Stage
seoDescription: How to build a 2027 apartment marketing plan around your lease calendar: which channels to fund at each lease stage, how to budget them and what to measure.
excerpt: Start the plan with your lease calendar, fund the channels renters use at each stage, and budget by the job each line has to do, not by a borrowed percentage.
imageAlt: Two coworkers placing sticky notes on a whiteboard labeled Marketing while teammates work on laptops in the background
imageIdea: Real photo of a small team planning on a whiteboard with sticky notes in an office, no visible brand logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
A 2027 apartment marketing plan should start with your lease calendar, then fund the channels renters use at each stage: finding you, choosing you, touring and renewing. Budget each line by the job it has to do and the months it has to do it in, not by a percentage borrowed from another portfolio.

I am not going to give you a percentage split. I have not seen a published, sourced benchmark for apartment marketing budgets that I would stand behind, and a split that suits a lease up in Phoenix is wrong for a stabilized garden community in Ohio. What I can give you is the structure we use when we plan with owners and asset managers.

What should a 2027 apartment marketing plan start with?

It should start with three numbers by month: expected move outs, units you need to lease and renewals coming due. A plan that ignores that calendar usually spends the most in the months it needs it least.

Pull lease expirations from your property management system and lay them across the year. Then look at your market's seasonality. RealPage's analysis of the prime leasing season found that the roughly April to September window still carried the majority of annual demand, though less sharply in 2023 than in earlier years, and that the first quarter averaged 12% of annual demand over the prior decade, excluding 2022. Your submarket may differ. The point is to know when a dollar has the most renters to reach.

Which channels belong in the plan?

Most communities need the same core set: a website that answers renter questions, a Google Business Profile someone owns, a review program, paid search, paid social run under housing rules, listing sites and a resident retention line. What changes by stage is how much of each and when.

  • Website. Fees, pets, parking, floor plans and availability in plain text. Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show a snippet to appear as a supporting link in its AI features.
  • Google Business Profile and Maps. Google says it weighs relevance, distance and prominence, and that more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking. Someone should own the profile every week.
  • Listing sites. In an Apartments.com survey reported by the National Apartment Association, 87% of more than 15,000 adults planning to rent had no specific property in mind when they started, and 85% said they use or plan to use a site like Apartments.com. Apartments.com ran the survey, so weigh it accordingly, but it explains why listings stay in most plans.
  • Paid search. Your brand name plus the unbranded searches renters use before they know you.
  • Paid social. Housing ads on Meta run in a Special Ad Category with fixed age and gender settings and no postal code targeting, so plan creative and geography for broad audiences.
  • AI answers. A monthly check of what ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity say about your community, and whether it is right.
  • Retention. Renewal communication, maintenance follow up and review replies. Keeping a resident is part of the marketing plan.

How should the plan change by lease stage?

Lease up plans pay for reach and speed, stabilized plans pay for efficiency and reputation, and renewal heavy months pay for retention. The channels overlap. The job of each dollar changes.

StageMain jobFund firstWhat to watch
Pre leasingGet found before openingWebsite, Google Business Profile setup, unbranded paid search, interest listInterest list growth, inquiries by source
Lease upLease units on schedulePaid search, paid social, listing sites, early reviewsLeases against plan, cost per lease by channel
StabilizedHold occupancy at lower costWebsite answers, Maps visibility, reviews, a smaller always on paid budgetOrganic and Maps share of leads, cost per lease
Renewal heavy monthsKeep residentsResident communication, maintenance response, review repliesRenewal rate, review themes

We go deeper on the first two rows in our posts on lease up marketing and Google Ads for lease up versus stabilized communities.

How should you set the budget without a percentage rule?

Cost each job, then check the total against your leasing goal. For every line, write what it must produce, in which months, and what you will cut if it does not.

  1. Fixed commitments. Website platform, listing contracts and reputation tools you are already signed into. Know the renewal dates.
  2. Owned work that compounds. Website answers, Google Business Profile upkeep and the review program. These keep working when paid spend pauses.
  3. Paid media on the lease calendar. Heavier in months with more units to lease, lighter when the rent roll is full.
  4. A flexible reserve. Money you can move when a competitor launches a concession or a building in your trade area opens.
  5. Measurement. Call tracking, form tracking and tour source fields that your leasing team actually fills in.

Ask every vendor to put a lease target or a leading indicator next to its line. If a vendor cannot say what its line should produce, that line is the first to question.

What should you measure each month?

Measure leases and tours by source, cost per lease by channel, and whether you show up for unbranded searches in Maps and AI answers. Clicks and impressions only matter if they move one of those. Our post on marketing metrics that predict leases lists the ones we use.

Every number in a monthly report should state the period it covers, and some months should show what did not work. A plan you can adjust is worth more than a plan that looks complete in January.

What changed going into 2027 that the plan should account for?

Two things: renters can now get answers about your community from AI tools as well as search results, and the fair housing rules for digital ads still apply even though HUD withdrew one piece of guidance. Plan time and money for both.

HUD's Federal Register notice withdrew its 2024 guidance on advertising housing through digital platforms, effective September 17, 2025. The Fair Housing Act itself and HUD's advertising regulation still apply, and Google still restricts how housing ads can be targeted in the United States and Canada. Build compliance review into the plan instead of treating it as a launch week task.

Questions we hear

What percentage of revenue should an apartment community spend on marketing?

I do not know of a published, sourced benchmark I would rely on, and the right amount depends on lease stage, market and how many units you need to lease each month. Cost each job against your leasing goal instead.

When should we build the 2027 marketing plan?

Once you have next year's lease expiration schedule and occupancy targets. Planning before those numbers exist means guessing which months need the most help.

Which channels matter most for a stabilized community?

Usually the owned ones: a website that answers renter questions, a Google Business Profile someone maintains, and a review program. Paid media still has a place, scheduled to the months with the most units to lease.

Do fair housing rules affect the marketing plan?

Yes. The Fair Housing Act applies to every ad, Meta runs housing ads in a Special Ad Category, and Google restricts housing ad targeting in the United States and Canada. Build review time into the plan.

How often should we revisit the plan?

Monthly, against leases and tours by source and cost per lease by channel. Move money when a line is not producing, rather than waiting for the next annual budget.

takeaways: Build the 2027 plan on your lease expiration and occupancy calendar before choosing channels.
RealPage found the roughly April to September window still carried most annual apartment demand, with the first quarter averaging 12% over the prior decade excluding 2022.
Budget each line by the job it must do and the months it must do it in, not by a borrowed percentage.
Measure leases and tours by source and cost per lease by channel every month, and move money that is not producing.
